content: The CDC revised its classification system for HIV infection in children in 1994, replacing the previous system from 1987. This updated system was developed to reflect the growing understanding of HIV disease progression in children. For the purposes of this classification, a child is defined as an individual under 13 years of age. Standard anti-HIV IgG antibody tests are not reliable for determining a child’s HIV infection status before 18 months of age due to the presence of maternal antibodies. Therefore, viral antigen tests are used for diagnosis in this age group. The revised classification system categorizes HIV-infected children into mutually exclusive groups based on three parameters. Additionally, the document includes updated pediatric definitions for two AIDS-defining conditions. Diagnosing HIV infection in infants born to HIV-infected mothers is particularly challenging because maternal anti-HIV IgG antibodies cross the placenta, resulting in nearly all such infants being HIV-antibody positive at birth. However, only 15%-30% of these infants are actually infected with HIV. Category N: Not Symptomatic Children in this category show no signs or symptoms attributable to HIV infection. Alternatively, they may have only one of the conditions listed under Category A. Category A: Mildly Symptomatic Children in this category exhibit two or more of the following conditions but none of the conditions listed under Categories B or C: Lymphadenopathy (enlarged lymph nodes measuring ≥0.5 cm at more than two sites; bilateral involvement counts as one site). Hepatomegaly (enlarged liver). Splenomegaly (enlarged spleen). Dermatitis (skin inflammation or rash). Parotitis (inflammation of the parotid glands). Recurrent or persistent upper respiratory infections, sinusitis, or otitis media (middle ear infections). Category B: Moderately Symptomatic Children in this category have symptomatic conditions that are not included in Categories A or C but are attributed to HIV infection. Examples of such conditions include: Persistent anemia (hemoglobin <8 g/dL), neutropenia (neutrophil count <1,000/mm³), or thrombocytopenia (platelet count <100,000/mm³) lasting at least 30 days. A single episode of bacterial meningitis, pneumonia, or sepsis. Oropharyngeal candidiasis (thrush) persisting for more than 2 months in children older than 6 months. Cardiomyopathy (disease of the heart muscle). Cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection with onset before 1 month of age. Recurrent or chronic diarrhea. Hepatitis. Recurrent herpes simplex virus (HSV) stomatitis (more than two episodes within 1 year). HSV bronchitis, pneumonitis, or esophagitis with onset before 1 month of age. Herpes zoster (shingles) involving at least two distinct episodes or affecting more than one dermatome. Leiomyosarcoma (a rare type of cancer affecting smooth muscle). Lymphoid interstitial pneumonia (LIP) or pulmonary lymphoid hyperplasia complex. Nephropathy (kidney disease). Nocardiosis (a bacterial infection). Persistent fever lasting more than 1 month. Toxoplasmosis with onset before 1 month of age. Disseminated varicella (complicated chickenpox). Category C: Severely Symptomatic Children in this category have severe conditions that are AIDS-defining. These include: Multiple or recurrent serious bacterial infections (e.g., septicemia, pneumonia, meningitis, bone or joint infections, or abscesses in internal organs or body cavities) confirmed by culture within a 2-year period. This excludes otitis media, superficial skin or mucosal abscesses, and infections related to indwelling catheters. Esophageal or pulmonary candidiasis (involving the bronchi, trachea, or lungs). Disseminated coccidioidomycosis (infection at sites other than or in addition to the lungs or cervical/hilar lymph nodes). Extrapulmonary cryptococcosis. Cryptosporidiosis or isosporiasis with diarrhea persisting for more than 1 month. Cytomegalovirus (CMV) disease with onset after 1 month of age, involving sites other than the liver, spleen, or lymph nodes. HIV-associated encephalopathy, characterized by at least one of the following progressive findings persisting for at least 2 months in the absence of another illness that could explain the symptoms: Failure to achieve or loss of developmental milestones or intellectual abilities, confirmed by standardized developmental scales or neuropsychological tests. Acquired symmetric motor deficits, such as paresis, abnormal reflexes, ataxia, or gait disturbances. Herpes simplex virus infection causing mucocutaneous ulcers persisting for more than 1 month, or bronchitis, pneumonitis, or esophagitis of any duration in children older than 1 month. Disseminated histoplasmosis (infection at sites other than or in addition to the lungs or cervical/hilar lymph nodes). Kaposi’s sarcoma. Primary brain lymphoma. Burkitt’s lymphoma, immunoblastic lymphoma, or large cell lymphoma of B-cell or unknown immunologic phenotype. Disseminated or extrapulmonary Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection. Disseminated Mycobacterium infections caused by species other than tuberculosis or unidentified species, involving sites other than the lungs, skin, or cervical/hilar lymph nodes. Disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) or Mycobacterium kansasii infection, involving sites other than the lungs, skin, or cervical/hilar lymph nodes. Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia (now known as Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia). Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (a rare brain infection caused by the JC virus). Recurrent nontyphoidal Salmonella septicemia. Toxoplasmosis of the brain with onset after 1 month of age. Wasting syndrome in the absence of another illness that could explain the following findings: Persistent weight loss exceeding 10% of baseline body weight. Crossing downward of at least two major percentiles on a weight-for-age growth chart (e.g., 95th, 75th, 50th, 25th, 5th) in a child older than 1 year. Chronic diarrhea (at least two loose stools per day for more than 30 days) or documented fever (intermittent or constant) lasting at least 30 days.
